title: Ambiguities & Saadianic Conventions
subtitle: מא לא ינקט — what the dots don't tell you
intro: The first three lessons taught the tidy version: one Hebrew letter, one gershayim, one Arabic sound. Real manuscripts and printed editions are messier. Scribes drop the dots, the same sound gets written two different ways, and Saadia spells some words by Arabic rules rather than Hebrew ones. None of this is hard once you know to expect it — and the tap-to-define reader resolves it for you. This lesson is the bridge from the chart to the page.

sections.heading: The dot is optional — so one letter, two sounds
sections.body: The gershayim that distinguishes خ from ك, ث from ت, ذ from د, غ from ج, ظ from ط is frequently left off — by scribes in a hurry and by typesetters alike. That means a bare letter can stand for either of two Arabic sounds, and you decide by the root and by the Hebrew it is translating. You already met خ as כ׳; here is the same word with the dot dropped.

examples.note: Fully it is כ׳לק (خ). With the dot dropped it looks identical to a word in ك — but the root √ḫ-l-q and the Hebrew ברא settle it.
Attested in the Tafsir with the خ written as a plain כ, no mark. Same letter, you supply the kh.
Dotted it is ת׳מר (ث). Undotted, it overlaps with תמר = تمر, 'dates' — context decides.
The everyday demonstrative; the ذ is so common it is constantly written as a bare ד.

sections.heading: Two conventions for the same sound
sections.body: Judeo-Arabic never had one committee. The same Arabic phoneme is written with different Hebrew letters in different traditions — and you will meet both. The two that matter most: خ (kh) and غ (gh).

examples.note: خ (kh) appears as ח׳ in many manuscripts (the form in Lesson 2) and as כ׳ in others, including this site's dictionary. Same sound, two letters.
The later, standardized convention writes غ (gh) as ע׳ (Lesson 2). The older, Saadianic convention writes it as ג׳ — the very mark that elsewhere means ج (j).
Because ג׳ can be ج in the later system and غ in the older one, this one symbol is genuinely ambiguous across traditions. Root and meaning disambiguate.

sections.heading: Saadia spells by Arabic rules
sections.body: Saadia's orthography (the classical Judeo-Arabic norm) follows Arabic spelling closely rather than writing things the Hebrew way. Three habits to recognize on sight.

examples.note: Final ـى (alif maqṣūra) is written with a yod — sometimes יod + gershayim (מוסי׳). It is an 'aa' sound, not 'ee'.
Final ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) is written with ה, exactly as it sounds in pause. In construct it can surface as ת.
Long ā is written plene with an alif (א), following Arabic spelling — not clipped as Hebrew might.

sections.heading: How to read when in doubt
sections.body: You do not need to memorize every variant. When an undotted letter could be two sounds, try both Arabic values, then let the triliteral root and the parallel Hebrew verse pick the winner — that is exactly how a trained reader does it. In this site's reader, tapping any word does that work for you: it gives the root, the normalized Arabic, and the gloss.

examples.note: Bare כלק: test ك and خ. Only √ḫ-l-q is a real verb meaning anything here, and the Hebrew is ברא. Answer: خ.
Bare תאבת: test ت and ث. The root √th-b-t ('be firm') is the live one.

quiz.q: Why can a single Hebrew letter stand for two different Arabic sounds in Judeo-Arabic?
choices: The distinguishing dot (gershayim) is often dropped
Hebrew has more letters than Arabic
quiz.explanation: The gershayim that separates خ from ك, ث from ت, etc. is frequently left off, so context and root must disambiguate.

quiz.q: Undotted כלק most likely represents which Arabic word?
quiz.explanation: The root √ḫ-l-q and the Hebrew ברא it renders point to خلق, 'he created' — the dot on כ has simply been dropped.

quiz.q: In the later standardized convention, غ (gh) is written as…
quiz.explanation: The standardized system writes غ as ע׳ (ayin + gershayim). The older Saadianic convention used ג׳ instead.

quiz.q: The Saadianic spelling מוסי ends in a yod. How is it pronounced?
quiz.explanation: The final yod writes alif maqṣūra (ـى), an ā vowel — Mūsā, 'Moses' — not an ī.

quiz.q: Final ة (tāʾ marbūṭa), as in سنة 'year', is normally written in Judeo-Arabic with which letter?
quiz.explanation: Tāʾ marbūṭa is normally written ה (סנה), matching its pausal pronunciation; in construct it can surface as ת.

quiz.q: You see the bare mark ג׳. Why is it ambiguous?
choices: It can mean ج (j) or غ (gh) depending on the tradition
It is never used in real texts
It only appears in modern Hebrew
It marks a vowel, not a consonant
quiz.explanation: ג׳ is ج in the later system but غ in the older Saadianic one — the same symbol, two values, resolved by root and meaning.
